newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: LABOR ASKS MORE QUESTIONS ON COLSTON

Labor Senators have raised more questions about Independent Senator, Mal Colston's use of travel allowance and entitlements. The Administrative Services Department is investigating Senator Colston's use of travel allowance and car entitlements.

In Senate estimates, Labor Senator Robert Ray, has asked if Senator Colston claimed travel allowance for being in Canberra but put out a press release saying he was on official business in Queensland.
Senator Colston says he's checking his movements on that date and says his claims for overnight allowances in Canberra are evidence he's a conscientious Committee Chairman.
Senator Ray has also asked if Senator Colston's son who worked for him, was asked to pay back travel allowance money in 1993.
HEPATITIS-A OUTBREAK SPREADS TO FIFTH STATE
The hepatitis-A outbreak, linked to the oysters from Wallis Lake on the mid north coast, appears to have spread to Western Australia.
It was confirmed yesterday that two West Australian men suffering from the disease, had eaten oysters believed to be from New South Wales.
Hundreds of cases of Hepatitis-A have already been reported to health authorities in in New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria and South Australia.
The West Australian Health Department recalled all Wallis Lake oysters imported into the state, but says there's a strong chance other cases will soon be reported.
NSW TAKES FIGHT TO VICTORIA IN BUSINESS WAR
New South Wales Premier Bob Carr says his state now provides the lowest cost environment for small business in Australia.
In using Victoria to prove his point, Mr Carr has resumed hostilties in the war of words over which state provides the best business climate.

Mr Carr compared Sydney and Melbourne's average power and water bills to show how Sydney was cheaper to operate in. Mr Carr also predicts the New South Wales government's real superannuation funding liabilities will start declining next year.
KENNETT STARTS REGIONAL TOUR
The Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, this morning starts a two-day visit to the state's north and north-east, insisting regional areas have done well out of his Government.

Mr Kennett will visit nine towns, including Cobram, Benalla, Euroa And Mansfield, and address a public meeting in Mansfield tonight. He says it's the first of several regional tours he'll make this year, because people off the beaten track are entitled to access to political leaders.
Despite the coalition's defeat in the West Gippsland by-election, Mr Kennett says his Government's policies have displayed a very positive bias towards regional Victoria.
He says employment and investment have grown at a greater rate than in Melbourne.
BUYING AUSTRALIAN PAYS OFF FOR FORD
Car-maker Ford Australia says the public's preference for the local product over imports was a major factor in a record profit achieved last year.
Ford's net earnings were up by $15 million to $217 million, in the second straight year of holding market leadership. Sales revenue was also a record, at $3.4 billion.
Ford President, David Morgan, says good profits have been essential for funding a huge investment in the next Australian Falcon.
NT PASTORAL LEASE NATIVE TITLE MEETING TODAY
Parties involved in a native title claim on a pastoral lease west of Tennant Creek in the Northern Territory are meeting today.

The claim is for compensation for loss of native title rights with the granting of the Suplejack Pastoral lease in 1993. The Native Title Tribunal, the claimants, the Central Land Council and representatives of the Territory and Commonwealth governments will set directions for a mediated agreement.
Compensation can be claimed for native title rights that have been lost since 1975, when the Racial Discrimination Act came into being.
ABORIGINES NEED TO CARE MORE ABOUT HEALTH: NT MINISTER
Territory Health Services Minister Denis Burke has called on Aboriginal people to take greater responsibility for their health.

Responding to a Parliamentary report into the Provision of Aboriginal Health Services in the Territory, Mr Burke said indigenous people have to care more about their health, by giving health a higher status.
Mr Burke said the major causes of Aboriginal hospitalisation are causes that can be fixed with remedies which are in the hands of the sufferer.
The Ministerial Statement delivered by Mr Burke was welcomed by Opposition Health spokesman Neil Bell.
ABORIGINAL GROUP LAUNCHING HEALTHY COOKBOOK
An Aboriginal group has produced a cook book, promoting a healthy diet.
Launching the book, New South Wales Aboriginal Affairs Minister, Andrew Refshauge, said the Koori Cook Book followed requests from Sydney's La Perouse Aboriginal community for tasty, health recipes.
Doctor Refshauge says because of the community's high rate of diabetes and other diet-related problems, the book is a practical way of improving health.
SA JUDGES TO HEAR ABORIGINAL VIEW ON JUSTICE
South Australian judges will hear from Indigenous people today about how they feel about the judicial system.
It's the second seminar organised for the state's judiciary since the Royal Commission into Black Deaths in Custody found Aboriginal people were confused and intimidated by the legal system.

A South Australian Supreme Court judge says some aspects of traditional Aboriginal law should be incorproated into the mainstream legal system. Justice Mullighan says in Aboriginal law, matters are resolved quickly and offenders are made to take personal responsibility for what they've done.
QUEENSLANDERS MAKE GENETIC BANANAS
Genetically engineered bananas could be on the nation's supermarket Shelves within five years with the production of Australia's first "test-tube" version of the fruit.

Researchers at Queensland University of Technology have spent the past three years cultivating banana plants from a single cell. Professor James Dale says in addition to allowing the development of more disease resistant banana strains, the research will help growers breed the fruit.
PM SHOULD BE PROTECTING HERITAGE, SAY CONSERVATIONISTS
Anti-Hinchinbrook Resort Development campaigner David Haigh, says it's not the job of developers or State Governments to protect World Heritage.

Mr Haigh says under the World Heritage Convention that responsibility lies with the Commonwealth. His comments follow a meeting between the Prime Minister, Queensland Premier, and developer Keith Williams about the future of the north Queensland resort. The meeting agreed to appoint an environmental monitor to oversee the development.
Mr Haigh says as head of the Government, Prime Minister John Howard if failing in his responsibility to adequately protect World Heritage values.
ACT TO REDUCE MASSIVE OPERATING LOSSES
An independent review of the ACT's finances has urged the
Government to significantly reduce massive operating losses to avoid long term pain for the Canberra community.

The Auditor-General says last year's operating loss of 347 million dollars and this year's projected loss of 232 million need to be addressed quickly. His report says continuing to defer superannuation payments will eventually force Governments to lift taxes or borrow in order to pay out retiring public servants. The Auditor also dismisses the Government's current economic strategies as insufficient to close the affordability gap, something Chief Minister Kate Carnell disputes.
COLLINS PRAISES FORMER NT ADMINISTRATOR
Territory Labor Senator Bob Collins has praised former Territoy Administrator Eric Johnston, who died yesterday, as a leader who kept in touch with the people.

Senator Collins says Commodore Johnston travelled to every corner of the Territory in a way that had been never done before, visting Every isolated community and pastoral property. Commodore Johnston died in Darwin yesterday, aged 63, and a State funeral will be held next Tuesday.
FIVE CAR PILE-UP IN NEW SOUTH WALES
Four people are in hospital after a five car smash at Toronto, near Newcastle in New South Wales.
One man was sent to hospital by helicopter and the other three were taken by ambulance.
GANG ATTACKS BUILDING IN ALICE SPRINGS
Residents of an apartment block on the outskirts of Alice Springs have been trapped inside their units tonight, as a rock-throwing gang smashed the building's windows.

Police say there were about 12 people in the group and estimate the the rampage caused two to three thousand dollars in damage. Police have been unable to locate the offenders, who ran off into the night when police arrived.
VICTORIA TEACHERS STRIKE OVER PUBLIC EDUCATION FUNDING

Victorian teachers will go on strike today over funding allocations. Education Union state president, Peter Lord, says the campaign is designed to pressure the Government into making public education a funding priority. But Education Minister, Phil Gude, says the Government has already increased funding to a range of programs and there could be more rises when the state gets a Triple A credit rating.
RECONCILIATION MEETINGS TO BE HELD THROUGHOUT NATION

The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation is holding public meetings around the country over the next six weeks. Council chairman, Pat Dodson, says they will open up widespread discussion about practical achievements for reconciliation, including the possibility of a national document.

The meetings are being held in every capital city and 23 regional centres, beginning in Albany, Western Australia. Mr Dodson says the public meetings are being held because the Council recognised most people would not be able to attend the Australian Reconciliation Convention, in May, which will chart the way forward for reconciliation.

He says while a document, in itself, cannot overcome the historical injustices experienced by many indigenous people, Australia needs a document of reconciliation as a foundation to advance the process.
